title: SQLite Small Examples
description: Use these small SQLite examples with the tools described in each lesson. Read the expected result before you try a change.

examples.title: Ask SQLite for an answer
examples.description: SQLite can calculate a value without a table.
examples.output: The result has one column named books_read with value 7.

examples.title: Create a sample table
examples.description: A table defines named columns for each record.
examples.output: The new sample table contains Moon Trip with id 1 and 60 pages.

examples.title: Inspect the kind of a value
examples.description: SQLite values have storage classes such as integer, real and text.
examples.code: SELECT typeof(12) AS whole,typeof(2.5) AS decimal_kind,typeof('12') AS words;
examples.output: The values are integer, real and text.

examples.title: Filter a query-only list
examples.description: WHERE chooses rows that pass a rule. A WITH list gives this practice query its own small dataset.
examples.code:
WITH books(title,pages) AS (VALUES('Moon Trip',60),('Tiny Seed',20))
SELECT title FROM books WHERE pages>=50;

examples.title: Sort and limit the result
examples.description: ORDER BY chooses the result order. LIMIT then keeps only the requested number of rows.
examples.code:
WITH books(title,pages) AS (VALUES('Moon Trip',60),('Tiny Seed',20),('Garden Days',40))
SELECT title FROM books ORDER BY pages,title LIMIT 2;
examples.output: Tiny Seed and Garden Days are returned in that order.

examples.title: Count a group of rows
examples.description: GROUP BY combines matching categories for a summary.
examples.code:
WITH books(kind) AS (VALUES('story'),('science'),('story'))
SELECT kind,count(*) AS total FROM books GROUP BY kind ORDER BY kind;
examples.output: Science has one book, and story has two.

examples.title: Join related records
examples.description: A join matches records using a rule. It can show an author name beside a title without repeating that name in every book record.
examples.code:
WITH authors(id,name) AS (VALUES(1,'Mia')),books(title,author_id) AS (VALUES('Moon Trip',1))
SELECT books.title,authors.name FROM books JOIN authors ON authors.id=books.author_id;
examples.output: The result pairs Moon Trip with Mia.

examples.title: Protect a positive number
examples.description: A CHECK constraint gives a rule for stored data.
examples.output: The sample value 5 is accepted. A negative points value would fail the check.

examples.title: Turn on foreign-key checks
examples.description: A foreign key links a child record to a parent id.
examples.output: The valid child row refers to reader 1. A row referring to a missing parent would be rejected with checks enabled.

examples.title: Undo an unfinished change
examples.description: A transaction can group row changes. ROLLBACK cancels uncommitted work inside that transaction.

examples.title: Inspect a table definition
examples.description: PRAGMA table_info shows facts about a table's columns.
examples.output: The result lists id and message with their types and column flags.

examples.title: Bind a value from Python
examples.description: An application should pass a value separately from SQL text.
examples.code:
import sqlite3
with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as connection:
    connection.execute("CREATE TABLE books(title TEXT)")
    connection.execute("INSERT INTO books VALUES (?)", ("Moon Trip",))
    print(connection.execute("SELECT title FROM books").fetchone()[0])
examples.output: Run with Python 3 to print Moon Trip from a temporary in-memory database.
